title: Why 'Healthy' Food Labels Don't Tell the Whole Story
paragraphs: When shopping for groceries, many people look for products with labels such as "low fat," "sugar free" or "reduced sodium." However, a new study from the United States suggests that these labels often do not tell the whole story about how healthy a product really is.

The study, which was published in the journal Nature Food in September 2026, was led by Miguel Gómez, a professor at Cornell University, and Pei Zhou, a postdoctoral researcher. The researchers analyzed nearly 150,000 food and drink products that were launched in the US over the past decade.

To judge how healthy the products were overall, the researchers used a system developed by the UK's Food Standards Agency. Unlike labels that focus on just one nutrient, this system gives a score based on a product's overall nutrition. It penalizes sugar, salt, saturated fat and calories, while rewarding fiber, protein, fruit and vegetables.

The results were surprising. Although half of the new products carried some kind of health claim on their packaging, two-thirds of all the products were found to be less healthy overall, including many of those with health claims.

The researchers discovered that companies often improve one aspect of a product while making another worse. For example, sodas labeled as having reduced sodium were more likely to contain extra sugar, while packaged meals with "no trans fat" labels often had more saturated fat and salt. Zhou described a reduced-fat cream cheese which, despite having less fat, contained more sugar and salt. The gaps were particularly large for drinks.
The researchers stressed that companies are not breaking the law. Health claims only need to be accurate about the specific nutrient they mention, not about the product as a whole.

In addition, words such as "natural" and "organic" are not official nutrition claims at all. However, previous research has shown that many shoppers believe these words mean a product is healthy. This is known as the "halo effect."

Gómez suggested that governments should consider labeling systems that reflect a product's overall nutrition, such as the warning labels used in Chile and Mexico. Meanwhile, the researchers advise shoppers to see claims on the front of a package as just a starting point and to check the full nutrition information on the back.
